newsitem.title: THAILAND: Khun Sa ill but business empire in Burma thriving.
newsitem.headline: Khun Sa ill but business empire in Burma thriving.

text.p: Former drug warlord Khun Sa, living in Burma under the supervision of its military rulers, has been struck by partial paralysis, but his business empire in Burma is thriving, an aide said on Friday.

The notorious former opium king of the Golden Triangle, which straddles the borders of Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, led his 20,000-strong Mong Thai Army (MTA) and cultivated opium poppies until his surrender to Burmese troops in January 1996.
"He is suffering from diabetes and his right hand is paralysed," the aide who was in Bangkok for a visit from Burma told Reuters.
Despite his sickness, the wealthy Khun Sa's vast commercial empire, including transport and hotel businesses in Burma, continued to operate smoothly, he added.
"The sickness will not impact on his businesses because all of them are run by a well-organised holding company," the aide said, declining to give details about the holding company.
Anti-narcotics sources, however, believed that the holding firm might be one in which some senior Burmese military figures may have interests.
Burma has refused a United States request to extradite Khun Sa on drug trafficking charges. U.S. authorities have offered a $2 million reward for his capture.

The ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) has said it will deal with Khun Sa under its own anti-drug laws and that he is under close government supervision. It has also declined to detail his whereabouts or activities.
The aide confirmed that Khun Sa, 62, operated a transport service from northern Mandalay and other northern areas to Rangoon, and ran hotel businesses.
"He has an 11-storey hotel under construction in Rangoon," he added, reaffirming that Khun Sa lived in a luxury house near Inya Lake, home to many of Burma's elite.
Burma's military government has repeatedly denied that Khun Sa is doing business in the country.

In his heyday, Khun Sa claimed that he was fighting for independence of his Shan state from the Burmese central government in Rangoon. But international anti-drug agencies accused him of using the MTA to protect his heroin business.
The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration estimates that about 70 percent of the world's heroin supply comes from the Golden Triangle.
Since Khun Sa's exit from the Shan area, the poppy growing and heroin trade has been taken over more actively by another dissident guerrilla group, the United Wa State Army, and remnants of the MTA.
